scenario.name: combined
scenario.description: Everything on: delays, revisions, delayed outcomes, several encounters, site differences.

target.definition: A simulated deterioration event with event time in (T, T + 12 h], in the same encounter as the prediction at time T.
target.prediction_schedule: Every 4 h from hour 4 of an encounter until it ends.
target.eligible_population: Predictions made while the patient is at risk: no earlier event in the encounter. Follow-up covers the full horizon for every prediction.
target.estimand: Discrimination, average precision and Brier score of a fixed model's predictions for the eligible predictions of held-out patients, under a stated feature-time policy.
target.average_precision_convention: Step-function average precision: sum over thresholds of (recall_k - recall_{k-1}) * precision_k. Not the trapezoidal area under the PR curve.

weighting: Metrics weight predictions equally unless marked patient-weighted.

experiment_a.question: With the model, prediction rows, labels and test patients held fixed, how much does the measured performance change when only the feature-time policy changes?
experiment_a.interpretation: Pipeline sensitivity of the evaluation. Not a comparison between independently trained models.

model.preprocessing: median imputation with missing-value indicators, then standardisation
model.selection_rule: lowest log loss on the validation patients

experiment_a.decomposition_note: revision_effect = latest_revised - pipeline_as_known (only the revision read changes). availability_effect = naive_event_time - latest_revised (only whether availability is respected changes). Their sum is the naive-minus-as-known gap. The split depends on the order in which the two changes are applied.

experiment_b.question: If the whole pipeline is built naively, how far is the number it reports from what the same model would achieve on features it could really have had, and does training on as-known features help at deployment?
experiment_b.design: Two models, same patients, same labels, same split, same model family and selection rule. Only the policy that prepared the training and validation features differs.
experiment_b.deployment_faithful_cell: any cell evaluated on as-known features

naive_trained.preprocessing: median imputation with missing-value indicators, then standardisation
naive_trained.selection_rule: lowest log loss on the validation patients

as_known_trained.preprocessing: median imputation with missing-value indicators, then standardisation
as_known_trained.selection_rule: lowest log loss on the validation patients

experiment_b.can_attribute: The contrasts isolate the effect of the feature-time policy on this cohort for these two fitted models.
experiment_b.cannot_attribute: Intervals are conditional on the two fitted models. They do not show that one training pipeline is better in general; that needs the variation across simulated cohorts reported in the cross-seed summary, and would need real data to say anything about a real system.

chronological.question: How would a model built from what was known at the cutoff date have performed on the patients who arrived afterwards?
chronological.differs_from_patient_holdout: The patient holdout asks about new patients from the same period. This asks about later patients. The simulation has no drift over calendar time, so no systematic difference between the two is expected here; the design is shown because real data would need it.

rules: A prediction is used for fitting only if its label was mature at the cutoff: prediction time + horizon + maximum ascertainment lag <= cutoff.
Fitting labels are computed from outcomes ascertained by the cutoff.
Test predictions are those after the cutoff from patients first seen after the cutoff.
A patient seen before the cutoff who returns afterwards is excluded from the test set.

model.preprocessing: median imputation with missing-value indicators, then standardisation
model.selection_rule: lowest log loss on the validation patients

subgroups.purpose: Descriptive only. No claim of fairness, clinical safety, or causal benefit.

label_maturity.purpose: Shows pending and unknown labels, and what is lost by labelling too early. The main analysis uses the completed study with mature labels.
label_maturity.premature_negatives_meaning: Predictions whose event happened inside the horizon but had not been ascertained when the horizon ended. A pipeline that labels as soon as the horizon elapses records each of them as a negative.

evaluation_against_impatient_labels.design: Frozen as-known model, as-known features, held-out test patients. Only the labels differ: mature labels of record versus labels recorded at T + H.

limits: All data are simulated. Nothing here is evidence about any real patient, hospital, or model.
The size and direction of every difference depend on the simulation's settings, which were fixed in advance and are not estimates of any real system.
Bootstrap intervals describe sampling variability in the test patients for models held fixed. They exclude the variability of model fitting and of the simulation itself.
A lower score under the as-known policy does not mean a worse engine. It means the naive number was measuring something the deployed pipeline could not have had.
Timestamp rules cannot establish clinical appropriateness, causality, or data validity.
Subgroup results are descriptive. They support no claim about fairness, safety, or benefit.
